stem: Which crop is a **perennial**?

options.rationale: Correct: citrus trees live and bear fruit for many years.
Maize completes its life cycle in one season, so it is an annual.
Onion naturally flowers in its second season, so it is a biennial.
Groundnuts are annuals harvested within one season.

explanation: Perennials live for more than two years; fruit trees such as citrus are typical examples.

stem: Which part of the Irish potato plant is eaten?

options.rationale: Correct: it carries buds (eyes), which only stems have.
Sweet potato and cassava are swollen roots; the Irish potato is not.
Bulbs, such as onions, are made of fleshy leaf bases.

options.content: A fruit formed from the ovary
options.rationale: The potato fruit is a small green berry and is poisonous, not the tuber.

explanation: The Irish potato is a swollen underground stem; its eyes are buds in the axils of scale leaves.

stem: A seedling has leaves with parallel veins and a fibrous root system. To which group does it belong?

options.rationale: Dicotyledons have net veins and a tap root.
Correct: parallel veins and fibrous roots are monocotyledon features.
Brassicas are dicotyledons with net-veined leaves.

options.content: Cucurbits, such as pumpkin and butternut
options.rationale: Cucurbits are dicotyledons with broad, net-veined leaves.

explanation: Monocotyledons (cereals and grasses) have one cotyledon, parallel veins, fibrous roots and scattered vascular bundles.

stem: Which group contains **only** solanaceous crops?

options.rationale: Cabbage is a brassica, not solanaceous.
Cotton and sweet potato belong to other families.
Correct: all three are in the potato family.
Pumpkin is a cucurbit.

explanation: Solanaceous crops include tomato, Irish potato, tobacco, pepper and eggplant; they share diseases such as bacterial wilt.

stem: Which crop is a **biennial**?

options.rationale: Sorghum is grown as an annual cereal.
Banana plants keep producing new suckers for years: a perennial.
Cowpeas complete their life cycle in one season.
Correct: it stores food in its first season and flowers in its second.

explanation: Biennials (carrot, onion, beetroot, cabbage) take two seasons to set seed; farmers harvest them after the first.

stem: Why should cabbages not be planted in a bed where rape was grown last season?

options.content: Rape takes all the nitrogen out of the soil, so nothing can grow there for a year
options.rationale: Rape uses nutrients, but this does not make the bed unusable.

options.content: Cabbages are monocotyledons, and they cannot follow a dicotyledon crop
options.rationale: Cabbages and rape are both dicotyledons; there is no such rule.

options.content: Both are brassicas, so pests and diseases of the rape may attack the cabbages
options.rationale: Correct: crops of one family share pests and diseases.

options.content: Rape releases a chemical that stops cabbage seeds from germinating at all
options.rationale: This is not the reason; cabbages are normally transplanted anyway.

explanation: Rotating crops between families breaks the cycles of pests and soil-borne diseases that attack one family.
hints: Think of the botanical family of each crop.

stem: A farmer sprays a selective herbicide on a maize field. The broad-leaved weeds die but the maize is not harmed. What explains this?

options.content: Maize is a perennial, so it can recover from the herbicide
options.rationale: Maize is an annual; recovery is not the reason.

options.content: The weeds are legumes, which are the only plants affected by herbicides
options.rationale: Herbicides are not restricted to legumes.

options.content: Maize leaves have net veins, which carry the chemical out of the leaf
options.rationale: Maize leaves have parallel veins.

options.content: The herbicide affects dicotyledons but not monocotyledons such as maize
options.rationale: Correct: many selective herbicides act on broad-leaved (dicotyledon) plants.

explanation: Selective herbicides use differences between monocotyledons and dicotyledons to kill broad-leaved weeds in cereals.
hints: Is maize a monocotyledon or a dicotyledon?

stem: Which crop is a **cucurbit**?

options.rationale: Covo is a brassica.
Correct: butternut is in the pumpkin family.
Eggplant is solanaceous.
Soya bean is a legume.

explanation: Cucurbits include pumpkin, butternut, watermelon, cucumber and squash.

stem: Cassava and sweet potato are grown for their swollen roots.
explanation: True. Both store starch in swollen roots; the Irish potato and yam are stem tubers.

stem: Vascular bundles are arranged in a ring in the stem of a monocotyledon such as maize.
explanation: False. In monocotyledons the vascular bundles are scattered; they form a ring in dicotyledons.

stem: Match each crop with the part that is eaten.
explanation: Onion: bulb of fleshy leaves. Sugar cane: stem. Rape: leaf. Tomato: fruit. Sorghum: grain.

stem: Match each crop with its botanical family.
explanation: Grouping by family helps to plan rotations, because members of a family share pests and diseases.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: A crop that completes its life cycle in one season is called an {{blank:a}}. A seed with two seed leaves belongs to a {{blank:b}}. Legumes carry nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Annuals live one season; dicotyledons have two cotyledons; legume root nodules hold Rhizobium bacteria.

stem: Name the family of crops that includes groundnuts, cowpeas and soya beans.
explanation: Groundnuts, cowpeas and soya beans are **legumes**: seeds in pods and nitrogen-fixing root nodules.

stem: State the type of root system found in a dicotyledon such as a bean.
explanation: Dicotyledons have a main **tap root** with lateral roots; monocotyledons have fibrous roots.

stem: State **four** differences between a monocotyledon and a dicotyledon.

points.description: One cotyledon in a monocotyledon seed; two in a dicotyledon.
Parallel leaf veins in a monocotyledon; net (branched) veins in a dicotyledon.
Fibrous roots in a monocotyledon; a tap root in a dicotyledon.
Scattered vascular bundles in a monocotyledon stem; bundles in a ring in a dicotyledon (or flower parts in threes versus fours or fives).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A monocotyledon has one cotyledon, parallel veins, fibrous roots and scattered vascular bundles; a dicotyledon has two cotyledons, net veins, a tap root and bundles in a ring.

explanation: Each difference must give both sides.

stem: Explain **two** ways in which classifying crops into botanical families helps a farmer.

points.description: Crops of one family share pests and diseases.
So the farmer rotates between families to break pest and disease cycles.
Legumes fix nitrogen.
So a cereal planted after a legume needs less nitrogen fertiliser (or: crops of a family need similar management, so planning and spraying are easier).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Crops in one family, such as tomatoes and potatoes, share pests and diseases, so planting a different family next breaks their cycles. Legumes fix nitrogen, so a cereal that follows them needs less nitrogen fertiliser.

explanation: Each use needs a reason.
hints: Think about pests, diseases and nutrients in a rotation.

stem: Tatenda plans to plant an orchard of mango trees. Explain **three** ways in which the perennial nature of mangoes affects his planning.

points.description: The land is occupied for many years, so a permanent, suitable site must be chosen.
There is no harvest for several years, so he needs money or other income until the trees bear.
The trees cannot be rotated, so long-term care is needed: protection of young trees, pruning, pest control and fencing.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The trees will stay in the field for many years, so he must choose a deep, well-drained permanent site. They will take several years to bear, so he needs other income until then. He cannot rotate the field, so he must plan for long-term pruning, protection and pest control.

explanation: Perennials need a long-term investment and permanent sites.
hints: How long is the land occupied, and when does income start?

stem:
A school garden near Mutare had these results last season.

| Bed | Crop grown last season | Problem seen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Tomatoes | Plants wilted suddenly; stems showed brown streaks inside |
| 2 | Cabbages | Many small holes in leaves; small green caterpillars |
| 3 | Maize | Good crop |
| 4 | Sugar beans | Good crop |

The garden committee must decide what to plant in each bed this season.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the botanical family to which the crop in bed 1 belongs.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which crop should **not** be planted in bed 1 this season?

options.rationale: Rape is a brassica and is not attacked by bacterial wilt of tomato.
A legume is a safe choice for bed 1.
Onion is from a different family and is a safe choice.
Correct: it is solanaceous and would be attacked by the same wilt.

parts.explanation: The wilt organism survives in the soil and attacks other solanaceous crops.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Bed 2 had cabbages. Name **one** other crop that should not follow them in that bed.
parts.explanation: Any brassica would share the caterpillar pests of the cabbages.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest which bed should be planted with maize this season and give a reason.

points.description: Bed 4 (after the sugar beans).
The legume left nitrogen from its root nodules, which the maize (a heavy nitrogen user) can use / maize follows a different family.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why rotating crops between botanical families reduces the problems seen in beds 1 and 2.

points.description: Pests and disease organisms attack crops of one family (a narrow host range).
Without a host crop from that family, they starve / die out / numbers fall.
So the next crop of that family, planted after a few seasons, is less attacked.

parts.explanation: Rotation removes the host and breaks the life cycle.

explanation: Identify the family of each crop, then use rotation between families to break pest and disease cycles and use legume nitrogen.
hints: Which beds held crops of the same family as the crop that had problems?
Legumes add nitrogen to the soil.

stem: A district extension leaflet lists the main types of crop grown locally: cereals, legumes, roots and tubers, and fruits.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: For **each** of the four types of crop, name one local crop and one product obtained from it.

points.description: Cereal, e.g. maize: mealie-meal / stockfeed / stover.
Legume, e.g. groundnut or soya bean: peanut butter / cooking oil / oilcake.
Root or tuber, e.g. Irish potato or cassava: chips / starch / food.
Fruit, e.g. orange or mango: fresh fruit / juice / jam.

parts.explanation: One crop and one product per type.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why growing a legume as well as a cereal improves a family's diet.

points.description: Legume seeds are rich in protein.
Cereals are mainly starch (carbohydrate), so legumes supply the protein that the cereal lacks.

explanation: Know the main local crop types, examples and products.
hints: Give one crop for each type and a product made from it.

stem: A farmer says: "It does not matter how I classify my crops. All that matters is that they grow." Discuss this view.

points.description: Family classification shows which crops share pests and diseases, guiding rotation.
Legumes fix nitrogen, so classification guides fertiliser savings in a rotation.
Monocotyledon/dicotyledon classification guides the choice of selective herbicides.
Life-cycle classification guides land use: perennials need permanent sites and long-term finance.
Part-eaten classification guides harvesting time, storage and marketing.
Judgement: the view is wrong; classification is a planning tool that improves yields and lowers costs.

levels.descriptor: Accurate, well-developed explanation of several relevant points using correct agricultural terms, applied to the crop, animal or situation in the question, with a clear judgement where one is asked for.
Some relevant points explained, partly developed or only partly applied to the situation; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation or application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The farmer is right that a good crop is the aim, but classification helps achieve it. Knowing families lets him rotate tomatoes away from potatoes, so soil-borne diseases die out, and put maize after beans to use the nitrogen fixed by legume nodules. Knowing that maize is a monocotyledon lets him use a selective herbicide that kills broad-leaved weeds only. Knowing that citrus is a perennial tells him it needs a permanent site and money to survive until the first harvest. So classification is not just theory: it is a planning tool, and the view is wrong.

explanation: Link each kind of classification to a practical decision, then judge.
hints: Think about rotation, pest control, herbicides and planning perennials.
